message.content: Explain the route table and what happens to a dead device.
Explain the route table and what happens to a dead device.

injected.body: A device that sends nothing for an hour is marked dead in the route table.
injected.label: Dead device

injected.body: The route table maps each device ID to the gateway nearest its grove row.
injected.label: Route table

injected.body: The router's queue holds at most ten thousand packets before it sheds the oldest.
injected.label: Queue limit

injected.body: The router drops any packet whose CRC-16 checksum does not match its payload.
injected.label: Checksum

injected.body: Device clocks drift a few seconds a day, so the router stamps packets on arrival.
injected.label: Clock drift

injected.body: A device resends a packet after eight seconds when no acknowledgement arrives.
injected.label: Retry window

injected.body: Gateways upload packets in batches every five minutes to save radio power.
injected.label: Batch upload

injected.body: Each sensor packet starts with a two-byte header naming the device and its firmware.
injected.label: Packet header

near_misses.body: Raising the gateway antenna two meters fixed the dropped packets from row twelve.
near_misses.label: Antenna fix

near_misses.body: Each gateway runs on a solar panel with a two-day battery.
near_misses.label: Gateway power

near_misses.body: A sensor in cold room B sends a packet when the temperature rises above two degrees.
near_misses.label: Storage sensor

part.content:
The route table is a data structure that maps each device ID to the gateway nearest its grove row. This allows signals or messages to be routed efficiently to the appropriate gateway associated with the device's location.

A device is considered dead if it stops sending any data for an hour. When a device is marked dead in the route table, it no longer participates in routing or communication until it becomes active again.

In summary:
- The route table links device IDs to their nearest gateways.
- If a device sends no data for an hour, it is marked dead in the route table.
- Dead devices are effectively excluded from routing until they resume activity.

Devices are mapped to gateways in the route table by their grove row. When a device is silent for an hour, it gets marked as dead and removed from active routing entries.
